questions.question: A polygon has 4 straight sides. Its side lengths are 12 cm, 5 cm, 12 cm and 5 cm, and all four of its angles are 90°. How should this polygon be sorted?
options: It is irregular, because its four sides are not all the same length.
It is regular, because a rectangle is a neat, familiar shape.
It is regular, because all four of its angles are equal.
It is regular, because it is closed and has four straight sides.
questions.explain: A polygon is regular only when BOTH attributes match: all sides equal AND all angles equal. Here the angles are all 90° but 12 cm and 5 cm are different, so it is irregular — the common trap is thinking a tidy, familiar rectangle must be regular.

questions.question: A polygon has 3 straight sides. Each side is 7 cm long, and each of its three angles is 60°. How should this polygon be sorted?
options: It is irregular, because a triangle does not look like a square.
It is regular, because all three sides are equal and all three angles are equal.
It is irregular, because only shapes with 4 or more sides can be regular.
It is regular, because it has three straight sides and is closed.
questions.explain: Check the two attributes: 7 cm = 7 cm = 7 cm and 60° = 60° = 60°, so this triangle is regular. The trap is judging by how familiar a shape looks — a triangle can be regular just as a square can.

questions.question: A polygon has 6 straight sides, and every side measures 5 cm. Its six angles measure 100°, 140°, 120°, 100°, 140° and 120°. How should this polygon be sorted?
options: It is regular, because all six of its sides are 5 cm.
It is regular, because a six-sided shape with equal sides is a familiar honeycomb shape.
It is irregular, because its angles are not all equal, even though its sides are.
It is irregular, because 5 cm sides are too short to make a regular polygon.
questions.explain: Equal sides alone are not enough — a regular polygon needs equal sides AND equal angles, and 100°, 140° and 120° are not all the same. The common trap is stopping after checking the side lengths.

questions.question: A polygon has 5 straight sides. Each side measures 4 cm, and each of its five angles measures 108°. Which statement about this polygon is true?
options: It is irregular, because it is not a square or a rectangle.
It is irregular, because 108° angles are not right angles.
It is irregular, because a regular polygon must have an even number of sides.
It is regular, because all five sides are equal and all five angles are equal.
questions.explain: All five sides are 4 cm and all five angles are 108°, so both attributes match and the pentagon is regular. Regular does not mean right angles or familiar-looking — it means every side equal and every angle equal.

questions.question: Four polygons are described by their measurements. Which one is a regular polygon?
options: Shape L: eight sides of 3 cm, with each angle 135°
Shape K: sides of 9 cm, 4 cm, 9 cm, 4 cm, with all four angles 90°
Shape M: sides of 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm, 2 cm, with angles that are not all equal
Shape J: four sides of 9 cm, with angles 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°
questions.explain: Only the eight-sided shape has every side equal (3 cm) and every angle equal (135°), so it is the regular one. Shapes that pass just one test — equal sides only, like the 9 cm four-sided shape, or equal angles only, like the 9 cm by 4 cm one — are still irregular.

questions.question: Nadia measures a polygon with 4 straight sides and finds that all four sides are 7 cm long. She wants to decide whether it is a regular polygon. What does she still need to check?
options: Nothing else — equal sides are enough to make a polygon regular.
Whether all four of its angles are equal.
Whether the shape looks like a rectangle, since rectangles are the regular four-sided shape.
Whether the perimeter is 28 cm.
questions.explain: Sorting by attributes takes two checks: sides and angles. Nadia's shape could be a slanted rhombus with equal 7 cm sides but angles of 60° and 120°, so she must measure the angles before calling it regular.

questions.question: For a math centre in Surrey, Owen puts four cut-outs into the bin labelled ‘regular polygons': a square with 5 cm sides and 90° angles; a triangle with three 8 cm sides and 60° angles; a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with 90° angles; and an eight-sided shape with 2 cm sides and 135° angles. Which cut-out does not belong in that bin, and why?
options: The eight-sided shape, because its 2 cm sides are shorter than the other shapes' sides.
The triangle, because a polygon with only three sides cannot be regular.
The rectangle, because its sides are not all the same length.
None of them — all four belong, because each one is a common, tidy shape.
questions.explain: The 10 cm by 4 cm rectangle has equal angles but unequal sides, so it fails the side-length attribute and is irregular. The trap is that a rectangle looks so tidy and familiar that children sort it as regular without measuring its sides.

questions.question: A polygon has 6 angles that all measure 120°, and its sides measure 4 cm, 4 cm, 7 cm, 4 cm, 4 cm and 7 cm. How should it be sorted?
options: Regular, because all six of its angles are equal.
Regular, because it is a familiar honeycomb hexagon shape.
Irregular, because the mode of its side lengths is 4 cm.
Irregular, because its sides are not all equal, even though its angles are.
questions.explain: Equal angles are only half the test — 4 cm and 7 cm sides are not all the same, so this hexagon is irregular. The trap is deciding from the angles alone, or from the shape's familiar honeycomb look.

questions.question: Jayden says the rectangular floor tile in his kitchen, 30 cm by 15 cm with four 90° angles, is a regular polygon because ‘a rectangle is the tidiest, most common shape there is.' Priya disagrees. Who is correct?
options: Priya, because a regular polygon needs equal sides AND equal angles, and 30 cm is not 15 cm.
Jayden, because rectangles are the neatest and most common shapes, so they count as regular.
Jayden, because the tile's four angles are all equal, and equal angles alone make a polygon regular.
Priya, because a polygon with four sides can never be a regular polygon.
questions.explain: Sort by attributes, not by how ordinary a shape looks: the tile's angles are all 90°, but 30 cm and 15 cm sides are unequal, so it is irregular. Note that a four-sided shape CAN be regular — a square is — so ruling out all four-sided shapes is also wrong.

questions.question: At a Kelowna craft fair, Mei buys a wooden coaster shaped like a polygon with 5 straight sides. She measures the perimeter and gets 40 cm, then measures one side and gets 8 cm. Is that enough for her to be sure the coaster is a regular pentagon?
options: Yes, because 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so every side must be 8 cm.
No — even if all five sides were 8 cm, she still has to check that all five angles are equal.
Yes, because a pentagon is a familiar shape, and familiar shapes are regular.
No, because the perimeter of a regular polygon must be an even number of centimetres.
questions.explain: A perimeter of 40 cm can be built from unequal sides such as 8, 8, 10, 7 and 7 cm, and even five equal 8 cm sides do not guarantee equal angles — both attributes must be checked. The trap is treating perimeter ÷ number of sides as proof that a shape is regular.

questions.question: Ms. Tran sorts polygons into two hoops. Hoop 1: a square with 5 cm sides and 90° angles; a triangle with 5 cm sides and 60° angles; a six-sided shape with 5 cm sides and 120° angles. Hoop 2: a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm with 90° angles; a four-sided shape with all sides 5 cm and angles of 50° and 130°; a five-sided shape with sides 5, 5, 5, 5 and 2 cm. What sorting rule is Ms. Tran using?
options: Hoop 1 holds shapes with 5 cm sides; Hoop 2 holds shapes with no 5 cm sides.
Hoop 1 holds shapes children see every day; Hoop 2 holds unusual shapes.
Hoop 1 holds shapes with equal sides AND equal angles; Hoop 2 holds shapes missing at least one of those.
Hoop 1 holds shapes with all angles equal; Hoop 2 holds shapes whose angles differ.
questions.explain: Test each rule against every shape: Hoop 2 also contains 5 cm sides and also contains the rectangle with all angles equal, so those rules break — only regular versus irregular explains both hoops. The trap is the everyday-shapes rule, since the familiar rectangle sits in Hoop 2, not Hoop 1.

questions.question: Kai compares two paper cut-outs for a math project at his school in Coquitlam. Shape A is a four-sided polygon with all sides equal and a perimeter of 36 cm. Shape B is a four-sided polygon with all four angles 90°, a perimeter of 36 cm, and one side that measures 12 cm. Kai says: 'They have the same perimeter, so both are regular polygons.' Which statement is correct?
options: Kai is right, because two polygons with the same perimeter must both be regular.
Both shapes are regular, because 36 ÷ 4 = 9, so every side of each shape is 9 cm.
Shape B is regular, because shapes with four square corners are the tidy, familiar kind.
Shape B is irregular — its sides must be 12 cm, 6 cm, 12 cm and 6 cm — and Shape A cannot be called regular until its angles are checked.
questions.explain: Work out Shape B's sides: the two 12 cm sides leave 36 − 24 = 12 cm for the other pair, so they are 6 cm each — unequal sides make it irregular even with four 90° angles. Shape A's sides are 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm each, but equal sides alone are not enough: it could be a slanted rhombus with 60° and 120° angles. Perimeter never decides regularity, and sorting the tidy right-angled shape as regular is the familiar-shape trap.
